FINDING_3_CB6b.issue: cibersort on degenerate eset_tme_stad 235x50 (12 LM22-overlap genes): 1-2/50 samples diverged (weights max 6.69e-05 QN=True; max 2.54e-04 QN=False)
FINDING_3_CB6b.mechanism: TWO independent last-bit input divergences vs the original pipeline, both amplified by the underdetermined 12-genes x 22-cell-types NuSVR (support-set flips), both absorbed by every well-posed case (hence 0 divergence on the 12 well-posed cibersort cases incl. 50181x50): (1) exp2: the original applies numpy's vectorized np.exp2; the crate used Rust libm f64::exp2, which differs by 1 ulp on ~5% of entries (measured: 594/11750 cells on the CB6b matrix, each 1 ulp). These last-bit mixture differences flow through QN/z-scores into the degenerate solve. (2) X scalar standardization: the reference X (pandas .loc -> to_numpy) is F-CONTIGUOUS, and numpy reduces a full-array sum over FLAT MEMORY ORDER (column-stacked) with the nditer reduce buffer (pairwise per 8192-element chunk, chunk sums accumulated sequentially). The crate used per-column sequential accumulation + pairwise over the 22 column totals: bitwise-equal on the official 531x22 matrix (coincidental at that size) but 1 ulp off on the 12x22 matrix (x_mean 1495.884602668057 vs ...567). Verified against X.mean()/X.std(ddof=1) on both matrices: flat-memory-order chunked pairwise is the exact match on both. The audit's 'N-dependent (>=21 columns) reduction' bisect signature was a red herring: with a FIXED 1-ulp input perturbation, whether a given sample's float32 weights/support set flips depends only on that sample's y values (which legitimately change with the column context through QN row means), so more context columns merely expose more knife-edge samples.
FINDING_3_CB6b.fix: exp2 heuristic + np.exp2 applied in the shim (numpy-exact, incl. np.max NaN propagation semantics), exp2_done flag added to cibersort_core; step-8 reduction rewritten to flat F-memory-order chunked pairwise

FINDING_4_CB11.gate: CB11 -> BOTH_ERROR_SAME_TYPE: ValueError 'Input y contains NaN.' on both sides

FINDING_5_quantile_normalize_np.issue: exposed helper disagreed with the numpy reference on the real 235x50 matrix (every cell, max abs diff 2679) while agreeing on transposes/random/small cases
FINDING_5_quantile_normalize_np.root_cause: NOT value-pattern-dependent (the audit's hypothesis) but LAYOUT-dependent: pd.DataFrame.to_numpy() returns an F-CONTIGUOUS array, and the helper's as_slice() handed back the raw column-major memory which the row-major Rust code silently misinterpreted (QN computed on effectively transposed memory). Any F-contiguous input was garbage; C-contiguous inputs (random arrays, ascontiguousarray copies) were bit-exact - which is exactly the observed agreement pattern.
FINDING_5_quantile_normalize_np.fix: kept in the public API (used only by iobrx/bench/bench_rust_cibersort.py QN-phase timing; nothing in the crate internals or other shims calls it - cibersort_core has its own internal quantile_normalize) and made layout-correct: values gathered through the ndarray view honoring strides; C-contiguous fast path unchanged
FINDING_5_quantile_normalize_np.gate: F-order direct, C-order, and F-order submatrix inputs all bitwise-equal to CS.quantile_normalize_fast on the real 235x50 exp2 matrix; cibersort_core and fit_nusvr_linear now fail loudly (ValueError) on F-order input instead of silently misreading

The original's error is a pandas .loc-expansion artifact inside its symbol-insert step, not a designed error contract; aligning the fast would mean re-introducing an upstream crash bug on input the fast handles correctly.
